presentingComplaint: Progressive swelling of both legs and around the eyes for 3 weeks, with frothy urine.
history: A 34-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of gradually worsening bilateral leg swelling and puffiness around the eyes, most noticeable on waking. He reports his urine has become persistently frothy, and he has had a 2-3 kg weight gain over this period. He denies gross haematuria, dysuria, fever, joint pains, oral ulcers, photosensitive rash, or recent sore throat/skin infection. No known diabetes, hypertension, hepatitis B/C, or HIV. No NSAID use. No history of recent vaccination, insect stings, or new drug exposure. No prior renal disease. Family history is non-contributory. He denies orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
examination: Alert, comfortable at rest. Bilateral pitting pedal and pretibial oedema extending to the shins, periorbital oedema, and mild ascites-like abdominal fullness. No skin rash, no joint swelling, no lymphadenopathy. Chest clear, no bibasal crackles. JVP not elevated. Abdomen soft, mild distension with shifting dullness suggestive of ascites; no organomegaly. No signs of DVT (calves non-tender, no unilateral swelling).

labs.urinalysis: 3+ protein, no dysmorphic RBCs, no red cell casts, occasional oval fat bodies/fatty casts

imaging: Renal ultrasound: both kidneys normal size, preserved cortical thickness, no obstruction
finalDiagnosis: Nephrotic syndrome, likely primary glomerular disease (pending renal biopsy and anti-PLA2R result)
citations: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Glomerular Diseases 2021
contraindications: Avoid empirical high-dose diuretics without correcting for intravascular volume status - risk of AKI/thromboembolism
Avoid NSAIDs (worsen renal perfusion and fluid retention)
Avoid unnecessary IV albumin infusion without concurrent diuretic and clear indication
edgeCases: If renal biopsy shows FSGS or minimal change disease, management/prognosis differs substantially from membranous nephropathy
Nephrotic syndrome carries hypercoagulable risk (renal vein thrombosis, DVT/PE) due to urinary loss of antithrombin III - vigilance required
Secondary causes (malignancy screening in older patients, hepatitis B/C, lupus, drugs) must be excluded before labeling as primary/idiopathic
This case (id: nephrotic) is captured in the diagnosable disease list only as a generic nephrotic syndrome entity - specific histological subtype is not separately coded
expectedMaiK: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and oedema in a normotensive, non-diabetic adult should prompt secondary-cause screening (ANA, hepatitis, HIV, anti-PLA2R) and renal biopsy referral; flag hypercoagulability and infection risk during work-up.

Any features suggestive of malignancy (age >50, weight loss, smoking history)?
Any joint pains, photosensitivity, oral ulcers suggesting lupus?
Any leg pain/swelling asymmetry or breathlessness suggesting venous thromboembolism?
Any family history of renal disease or deafness (Alport)?
